<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.p6.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p6.3.1" class="ltx_text">respectively.
The first of these cyclic groups is a subgroup of <math id="S2.p6.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="SU(2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">SU(2)</annotation></semantics></math>, and so gives rise to a singularity of <span id="S2.p6.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_sansserif">type T</span>, modeled on the tangent cone at infinity of
a gravitational instanton of type
<math id="S2.p6.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{p-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{p-1}</annotation></semantics></math>. However, the other two singularities are not of <span id="S2.p6.3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_sansserif">type T</span>, because in both cases the relevant cyclic group is not contained in
<math id="S2.p6.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="SU(2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">SU(2)</annotation></semantics></math>, and its order is not divisible by a square. These Kähler-Einstein orbifolds <math id="S2.p6.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="({\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2},g_{FS})/{\mathbb{Z}}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">({\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2},g_{FS})/{\mathbb{Z}}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> can therefore never be limits
of admissible sequences of smooth Einstein manifolds.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Indeed, this set of examples also leads to a stronger conclusion:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmthm4" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_prop">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmthm4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 2.4</span></span><span id="S2.Thmthm4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S2.Thmthm4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmthm4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmthm4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Either there are infinitely many topological types of compact Kähler-Einstein orbifolds <math id="S2.Thmthm4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,g_{\infty})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X,g_{\infty})</annotation></semantics></math> with isolated singularities
that cannot arise as Gromov-Hausdorff limits of smooth Einstein manifolds,
or else there are Ricci-flat ALE <math id="S2.Thmthm4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifolds that remain to be discovered.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.3" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="S2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text">If we assume that we already know all possible Ricci-flat ALE <math id="S2.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifolds,
the only additional freedom allowed beyond the <span id="S2.p8.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_sansserif">type T</span> scenario is that some of the Ricci-flat
Kähler gravitational instantons might arise with the non-standard orientation, thus
allowing them to have <math id="S2.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{-}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{-}=0</annotation></semantics></math> instead of <math id="S2.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{+}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{+}=0</annotation></semantics></math>. However, for any prime <math id="S2.p8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>, this would still only allow
<math id="S2.p8.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{Z}}_{p}\subset\mathbf{U}(2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>⊂</mo><mrow><mi>𝐔</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{Z}}_{p}\subset\mathbf{U}(2)</annotation></semantics></math> to arise in connection to an orbifold singularity <math id="S2.p8.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{C}^{2}/{\mathbb{Z}}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>ℂ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{C}^{2}/{\mathbb{Z}}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> if the
<math id="S2.p8.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{Z}}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{Z}}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> action were generated by</span></p>
<table id="S2.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\eta&amp;\\
&amp;\eta^{-1}\end{array}\right]\mbox{ or }\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\eta&amp;\\
&amp;\eta\end{array}\right]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>[</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><mi>η</mi></mtd><mtd></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd></mtd><mtd><msup><mi>η</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext> or </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><mi>η</mi></mtd><mtd></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd></mtd><mtd><mi>η</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\eta&amp;\\
&amp;\eta^{-1}\end{array}\right]\mbox{ or }\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\eta&amp;\\
&amp;\eta\end{array}\right]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.p8.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p8.2.1" class="ltx_text">for some <math id="S2.p8.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p^{\rm th}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>p</mi><mi>th</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p^{\rm th}</annotation></semantics></math> root of unity <math id="S2.p8.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math>.
However, for any prime <math id="S2.p8.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\geq 5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\geq 5</annotation></semantics></math>, two of the singularities of the isometric quotients <math id="S2.p8.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}/{\mathbb{Z}}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}/{\mathbb{Z}}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> discussed above are certainly not of this form.
Thus, these examples cannot be Gromov-Hausdorff limits of sequences of smooth Einstein <math id="S2.p8.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifolds unless there are undiscovered ALE gravitational
instantons that are not half-conformally-flat.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Of course, the examples displayed in the proof of Proposition <a href="#S2.Thmthm3" title="Proposition 2.3. ‣ 2 Singularities of Type T ‣ Desingularizations of ConformallyKähler, Einstein Orbifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a> are just the tip of the iceberg. Even among cyclic quotients of
<math id="S2.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, one could either replace the prime <math id="S2.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> with an arbitrary product of distinct primes, or change the specific powers of the root of unity
<math id="S2.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math> in the matrix that generates the action. Another family of examples that would have sufficed to prove Proposition
<a href="#S2.Thmthm3" title="Proposition 2.3. ‣ 2 Singularities of Type T ‣ Desingularizations of ConformallyKähler, Einstein Orbifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a> can be obtained by
instead dividing the product Einstein metric on <math id="S2.p9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{1}\times{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>ℂ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{1}\times{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> by the action of a cyclic group <math id="S2.p9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{Z}}_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{Z}}_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.p9.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\neq 2,4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\neq 2,4</annotation></semantics></math>, acting on both <math id="S2.p9.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> factors by identical rotations
about an axis;
these examples have four orbifold singularities, but only two of them are of <span id="S2.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_sansserif">type T</span>.
For an infinite class of non-locally-symmetric Kähler-Einstein examples with
singularities that are not of <span id="S2.p9.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_sansserif">type T</span>, see <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>.
For non-Kähler examples of compact <math id="S2.p9.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional Hermitian Einstein orbifolds which have singularities that are not of <span id="S2.p9.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_sansserif">type T</span>, see <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Hermitian, Einstein Orbifolds</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While Theorem <a href="#Thmmain1" title="Theorem A. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Desingularizations of ConformallyKähler, Einstein Orbifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a> just concerns the case where <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,g_{\infty})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X,g_{\infty})</annotation></semantics></math> is a Kähler-Einstein orbifold with <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>,
Theorem <a href="#Thmmain2" title="Theorem B. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Desingularizations of ConformallyKähler, Einstein Orbifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> weakens this hypothesis by merely requiring that the <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> Einstein orbifold <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,g_{\infty})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X,g_{\infty})</annotation></semantics></math> be Hermitian. Let us therefore point out that this weaker condition can be restated in various equivalent ways.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmthm1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_thm">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmthm1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 3.1</span></span><span id="S3.Thmthm1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmthm1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmthm1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmthm1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A compact oriented
simply-connected
<math id="S3.Thmthm1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> Einstein orbifold <math id="S3.Thmthm1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X^{4},g)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X^{4},g)</annotation></semantics></math>
is Hermitian, in the sense that <math id="S3.Thmthm1.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="g=g(J\cdot,J\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>J</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>J</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=g(J\cdot,J\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> for some integrable orientation-compatible orbifold complex structure <math id="S3.Thmthm1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="S3.Thmthm1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math>,
if and only if one of the following equivalent conditions holds:</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmthm1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S3.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(i)</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The Einstein metric </span><math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> is conformally Kähler, meaning that there is a smooth positive function
</span><math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u:X\to{\mathbb{R}}^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u:X\to{\mathbb{R}}^{+}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> such that </span><math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\check{g}=u^{2}g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>ˇ</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\check{g}=u^{2}g</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> is
a Kähler metric with respect to some orientation-compatible integrable orbifold complex structure </span><math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> on </span><math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">.</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(ii)</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The self-dual Weyl curvature </span><math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{+}:\Lambda^{+}\to\Lambda^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{+}:\Lambda^{+}\to\Lambda^{+}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> of </span><math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> has two equal, negative eigenvalues at almost every point
of </span><math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">.</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(iii)</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">There is a global self-dual harmonic </span><math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">-form </span><math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ω</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> on the compact orbifold </span><math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,g)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X,g)</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> such that </span><math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{+}(\omega,\omega)&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{+}(\omega,\omega)&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> at every
point of </span><math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">.</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(iv)</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The self-dual Weyl curvature </span><math id="S3.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{+}:\Lambda^{+}\to\Lambda^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{+}:\Lambda^{+}\to\Lambda^{+}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> satisfies </span><math id="S3.I1.i4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\det(W^{+})&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0em">det</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\det(W^{+})&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> at every point of </span><math id="S3.I1.i4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">.</span></p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.1" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">If the Einstein orbifold <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,g)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X,g)</annotation></semantics></math> satisfies condition (<a href="#S3.I1.i1" title="item i ‣ Theorem 3.1. ‣ 3 Hermitian, Einstein Orbifolds ‣ Desingularizations of ConformallyKähler, Einstein Orbifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">i</span></a>),
the Riemannian Goldberg-Sachs theorem implies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite> that it either
satisfies condition (<a href="#S3.I1.i2" title="item ii ‣ Theorem 3.1. ‣ 3 Hermitian, Einstein Orbifolds ‣ Desingularizations of ConformallyKähler, Einstein Orbifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">ii</span></a>), or else satisfies <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{+}\equiv 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>≡</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{+}\equiv 0</annotation></semantics></math>. However, the compactness of <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> and the positivity of the
Ricci curvature of <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> together exclude the latter possibility,
because
the orbifold generalization of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, Theorem 1]</cite> and the fact that <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{1}(X)=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{1}(X)=0</annotation></semantics></math>
would then imply that <math id="S3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> is globally conformal to a scalar-flat Kähler orbifold metric,
contradicting the assumption that <math id="S3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> has positive scalar curvature.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text">The characterization (<a href="#S3.I1.i2" title="item ii ‣ Theorem 3.1. ‣ 3 Hermitian, Einstein Orbifolds ‣ Desingularizations of ConformallyKähler, Einstein Orbifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">ii</span></a>)
of conformally Kähler, Einstein metrics is due to Derdziński <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>, and is strictly
local; the proof moreover shows that if this eigenvalue condition holds on a dense set, it
actually holds everywhere. When this happens, the Kähler metric <math id="S3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\check{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>ˇ</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\check{g}</annotation></semantics></math> is actually
</span><span id="S3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">extremal</span><span id="S3.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text"> in the sense of Calabi; and, after possibly replacing it with a constant multiple,
one can arrange for the scalar curvature <math id="S3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{\check{g}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>ˇ</mo></mover></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{\check{g}}</annotation></semantics></math> of this extremal Kähler metric to exactly equal the positive
function <math id="S3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text">If criterion (<a href="#S3.I1.i3" title="item iii ‣ Theorem 3.1. ‣ 3 Hermitian, Einstein Orbifolds ‣ Desingularizations of ConformallyKähler, Einstein Orbifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">iii</span></a>) is satisfied, then, since the orbifold <math id="S3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> is assumed to be compact, the Weitzenböck-formula proof of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, Theorem 1]</cite> works exactly as in the manifold case. This then shows that the conformally related metric
for which <math id="S3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\omega|\equiv\sqrt{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≡</mo><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\omega|\equiv\sqrt{2}</annotation></semantics></math> must actually be Kähler.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text">Criterion (<a href="#S3.I1.i4" title="item iv ‣ Theorem 3.1. ‣ 3 Hermitian, Einstein Orbifolds ‣ Desingularizations of ConformallyKähler, Einstein Orbifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">iv</span></a>) was first proposed by
Peng Wu <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite>. If <math id="S3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha:X\to{\mathbb{R}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha:X\to{\mathbb{R}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the positive eigenvalue of <math id="S3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{+}</annotation></semantics></math>, the proof in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> shows that <math id="S3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h=\alpha^{2/3}g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>α</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h=\alpha^{2/3}g</annotation></semantics></math>
is Kähler, using a Wetizenböck argument that works just as well on a compact orbifold as it does on a compact manifold.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Constraints on Diffeotype</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Next, we completely classify the smooth closed <math id="S4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifolds that carry admissible sequences of Einstein metrics for which the limit is
conformally Kähler.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.Thmthm1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_thm">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S4.Thmthm1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 4.1</span></span><span id="S4.Thmthm1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S4.Thmthm1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Suppose that <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> is a smooth compact oriented <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifold that admits an admissible sequence <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> of
Einstein metrics such that
<math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{(M,g_{i})\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{(M,g_{i})\}</annotation></semantics></math> Gromov-Hausdorff converges to
a Hermitian, Einstein orbifold <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X^{4},g_{\infty})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X^{4},g_{\infty})</annotation></semantics></math> with Einstein constant <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>.
Then <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> is necessarily diffeomorphic to a Del Pezzo surface. In other words, <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> is diffeomorphic either to <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}\times S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}\times S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>
or to
a connected sum <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}\#\ell\overline{{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">#</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℙ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}\#\ell\overline{{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> for some
<math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell\in\{0,1,\ldots,8\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell\in\{0,1,\ldots,8\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
In particular,
<math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{1}(M)=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{1}(M)=0</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{+}(M)=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{+}(M)=1</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.Thmthm1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{-}(M)\leq 8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mo>−</mo></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{-}(M)\leq 8</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.1" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">As we previously saw in the proof of Proposition <a href="#S2.Thmthm2" title="Proposition 2.2. ‣ 2 Singularities of Type T ‣ Desingularizations of ConformallyKähler, Einstein Orbifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>, <math id="S4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> must be diffeomorphic to the manifold obtained by replacing each orbifold singularity of <math id="S4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> with a Ricci-flat Kähler
ALE manifold. Each such replacement is implemented <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite> by cutting out a small distance ball around a singular point <math id="S4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{k}\in X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{k}\in X</annotation></semantics></math>,
thereby introducing a boundary modeled on a spherical space-form <math id="S4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}/\Gamma_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>/</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}/\Gamma_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, and then
gluing in a truncation of a Ricci-flat anti-self-dual ALE manifold <math id="S4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(Y_{k},\mathsf{h}^{(k)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝗁</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(Y_{k},\mathsf{h}^{(k)})</annotation></semantics></math> for which a neighborhood of infinity is modeled on <math id="S4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(S^{3}/\Gamma_{k})\times{\mathbb{R}}^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>/</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(S^{3}/\Gamma_{k})\times{\mathbb{R}}^{+}</annotation></semantics></math>.
If <math id="S4.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Gamma_{k}\subset SU(2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>⊂</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Gamma_{k}\subset SU(2)</annotation></semantics></math>, so that <math id="S4.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(Y_{k},\mathsf{h}^{(k)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝗁</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(Y_{k},\mathsf{h}^{(k)})</annotation></semantics></math> is hyper-Kähler, choose
a compatible integrable almost-complex structure <math id="S4.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>J</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math> which is asymptotic to the obvious one on <math id="S4.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{C}^{2}/\Gamma_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>ℂ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>/</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{C}^{2}/\Gamma_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>; otherwise,
when <math id="S4.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Gamma_{k}\subset U(2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>⊂</mo><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Gamma_{k}\subset U(2)</annotation></semantics></math> but <math id="S4.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> is not simply connected, there is still an integrable almost-complex structure <math id="S4.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>J</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math> that is
analogously asymptotic to the obvious choice. Because <math id="S4.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathsf{h}^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝗁</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{h}^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math> is ALE of order <math id="S4.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>, we thus have <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite></span></p>

<p id="S4.p2.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p2.3.1" class="ltx_text">where <math id="S4.p2.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varrho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϱ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varrho</annotation></semantics></math> is the usual Euclidean radius, <math id="S4.p2.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ω</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math> is the Kähler form of <math id="S4.p2.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(Y_{k},\mathsf{h}^{(k)},J^{(k)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝗁</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>J</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(Y_{k},\mathsf{h}^{(k)},J^{(k)})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.p2.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega^{0}=dx^{1}\wedge dy^{1}+dx^{2}\wedge dy^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>ω</mi><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><mo>∧</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>∧</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega^{0}=dx^{1}\wedge dy^{1}+dx^{2}\wedge dy^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is the standard orbifold symplectic structure on <math id="S4.p2.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{C}^{2}/\Gamma_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>ℂ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>/</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{C}^{2}/\Gamma_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>.
A quantitative refinement of the standard Moser stability argument then shows <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>, Proposition 1.1]</cite> that, for each <math id="S4.p2.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>, there is
a diffeomorphism <math id="S4.p2.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Psi=\Psi^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Psi=\Psi^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math> defined on some asymptotic
region <math id="S4.p2.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varrho&gt;{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϱ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varrho&gt;{A}</annotation></semantics></math> with</span></p>
<table id="S4.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
