</table>
<p id="S4.p2.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p2.4.1" class="ltx_text">Thus, for a large constant <math id="S4.p2.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C\gg 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>≫</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C\gg 0</annotation></semantics></math> and a suitably small <math id="S4.p2.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ε</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>,
the composition of <math id="S4.p2.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Psi</annotation></semantics></math> with multiplication by <math id="S4.p2.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C/\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>ε</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C/\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math> defines
a symplectomorphism between the tiny annular region
<math id="S4.p2.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon&lt;\varrho&lt;2\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ε</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>ϱ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ε</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon&lt;\varrho&lt;2\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math> in <math id="S4.p2.m29" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathbb{C}^{2}/\Gamma_{k},\omega_{0})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℂ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>/</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ω</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbb{C}^{2}/\Gamma_{k},\omega_{0})</annotation></semantics></math> and the annular region in
<math id="S4.p2.m30" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(Y_{k},\varepsilon^{2}C^{-2}\omega^{(k)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ε</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ω</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(Y_{k},\varepsilon^{2}C^{-2}\omega^{(k)})</annotation></semantics></math> that is the image under <math id="S4.p2.m31" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Psi</annotation></semantics></math> of the annulus <math id="S4.p2.m32" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C&lt;\varrho&lt;2C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>ϱ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C&lt;\varrho&lt;2C</annotation></semantics></math>.
Identifying the domain of this map with a tiny annulus about the orbifold singularity <math id="S4.p2.m33" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{k}\in X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{k}\in X</annotation></semantics></math> then shows that
the Kähler form on <math id="S4.p2.m34" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,g_{\infty})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X,g_{\infty})</annotation></semantics></math> can be extended across <math id="S4.p2.m35" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> as a symplectic form. Since the map
used here to attach <math id="S4.p2.m36" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> to the regular part of <math id="S4.p2.m37" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> is moreover isotopic to the one used to reconstruct <math id="S4.p2.m38" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> from <math id="S4.p2.m39" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> and the <math id="S4.p2.m40" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>,
applying this same procedure
to all of the orbifold singularities of <math id="S4.p2.m41" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> therefore constructs a symplectic form <math id="S4.p2.m42" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ω</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega</annotation></semantics></math> on a manifold diffeomorphic to <math id="S4.p2.m43" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text">It follows that the smooth compact <math id="S4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifold <math id="S4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> admits both a symplectic form <math id="S4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ω</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega</annotation></semantics></math> and an Einstein metric <math id="S4.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> of positive Einstein constant.
This implies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite> that <math id="S4.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> must be diffeomorphic to a Del Pezzo surface. Indeed, since <math id="S4.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> admits both a symplectic form and
a metric of positive scalar curvature,
Seiberg-Witten theory implies that it contains a pseudoholomorphic <math id="S4.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>-sphere of non-negative self-intersection, and so
must be symplectomorphic to a rational or ruled complex surface <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>, <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>. The fact that <math id="S4.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> must also <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> satisfy the strict
Hitchin-Thorpe inequality <math id="S4.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(2\chi+3\tau)(M)=c_{1}^{2}(M)&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(2\chi+3\tau)(M)=c_{1}^{2}(M)&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> then narrows the list of possibilities down to the Del Pezzo diffeotypes.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This result is nominally sharp, since
every Del Pezzo <math id="S4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifold <math id="S4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> actually does
admit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> conformally Kähler, positive-<math id="S4.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> Einstein metrics <math id="S4.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>, and therefore
admits admissible <span id="S4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_sansserif">constant</span>
sequences <math id="S4.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{i}=g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{i}=g</annotation></semantics></math> with limit <math id="S4.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,g)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,g)</annotation></semantics></math>. However, this tautological construction of course never yields sequences that
converge to singular orbifolds. In fact, we will eventually see that demanding that <math id="S4.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> have at least one
singular point actually winnows the list down
to the four diffeotypes <math id="S4.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}\#\ell\overline{{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ℙ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>#</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>ℂ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ℙ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}_{2}\#\ell\overline{{\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\leq\ell\leq 8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\leq\ell\leq 8</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We have already seen that most Kähler-Einstein orbifold complex surfaces certainly cannot arise as limits of admissible sequences
of Einstein manifolds. This is partly explained by the fact that the first Chern class <math id="S4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{1}=c_{1}^{\rm orb}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>orb</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{1}=c_{1}^{\rm orb}</annotation></semantics></math> of such an orbifold <math id="S4.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math>
is usually only defined as an element of <math id="S4.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{2}(X,{\mathbb{Q}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ℚ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{2}(X,{\mathbb{Q}})</annotation></semantics></math>, and that its self-intersection <math id="S4.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{1}^{2}(X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{1}^{2}(X)</annotation></semantics></math> is therefore in general only a rational number.
When the orbifold is the limit of an admissible sequence, however, the situation is drastically simpler.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.Thmthm2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_prop">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S4.Thmthm2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 4.2</span></span><span id="S4.Thmthm2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S4.Thmthm2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">If a Hermitian, <math id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> Einstein orbifold <math id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X^{4},J,g_{\infty})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>J</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X^{4},J,g_{\infty})</annotation></semantics></math> is the Gromov-Hausdorff limit of an admissible sequence <math id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,g_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,g_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>
of smooth Einstein <math id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifolds <math id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,g_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,g_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>, then
<math id="S4.Thmthm2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{1}^{2}(X,J)=(2\chi+3\tau)(M)\in\{1,2,3,4,\ldots,9\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{1}^{2}(X,J)=(2\chi+3\tau)(M)\in\{1,2,3,4,\ldots,9\}</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="S4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text">We have just seen that <math id="S4.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\approx(X-\{p_{k}\})\cup\coprod_{k}Y_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em">∪</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∐</mo><mi>k</mi></msub><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\approx(X-\{p_{k}\})\cup\coprod_{k}Y_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, where each <math id="S4.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> is a singular point of <math id="S4.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math>, and where
<math id="S4.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> is a corresponding gravitational instanton. Moreover, each overlap <math id="S4.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X-\{p_{k}\})\cap Y_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∩</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X-\{p_{k}\})\cap Y_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> is diffeomorphic to
<math id="S4.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{R}}\times(S^{3}/\Gamma_{k})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ℝ</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>/</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{R}}\times(S^{3}/\Gamma_{k})</annotation></semantics></math> for an appropriate finite group <math id="S4.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Gamma_{k}\subset U(2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>⊂</mo><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Gamma_{k}\subset U(2)</annotation></semantics></math> that acts freely on <math id="S4.p6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>. Finally, we have seen that
<math id="S4.p6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>
admits a symplectic structure <math id="S4.p6.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ω</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega</annotation></semantics></math> that is symplectically isotopic to the Kähler form of <math id="S4.p6.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(J,g_{\infty})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>J</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(J,g_{\infty})</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="S4.p6.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X-\{p_{k}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X-\{p_{k}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, and that
is symplectically isotopic to the Kähler form of a Ricci-flat Kähler metric on each <math id="S4.p6.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>. This in particular implies that there exists
a positive integer <math id="S4.p6.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> such that the <math id="S4.p6.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m^{\rm th}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>m</mi><mi>th</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m^{\rm th}</annotation></semantics></math> tensor power <math id="S4.p6.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K^{-m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K^{-m}</annotation></semantics></math> of the anti-canonical line bundle <math id="S4.p6.m17" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="K^{-1}=\wedge^{2}T^{1,0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em">∧</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>T</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K^{-1}=\wedge^{2}T^{1,0}</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S4.p6.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,\omega)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,\omega)</annotation></semantics></math> is
trivial on each <math id="S4.p6.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, and is bundle-isomorphic to the dual of the pluricanonical line bundle <math id="S4.p6.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K^{\otimes m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K^{\otimes m}</annotation></semantics></math> on the regular part <math id="S4.p6.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X-\{p_{k}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X-\{p_{k}\}</annotation></semantics></math>
of <math id="S4.p6.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math>. Let us now choose a generic smooth section of <math id="S4.p6.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S4.p6.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K^{-m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K^{-m}</annotation></semantics></math> which is non-zero on each <math id="S4.p6.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> and
meets the zero section of <math id="S4.p6.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K^{-m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K^{-m}</annotation></semantics></math> transversely along a compatibly-oriented compact surface <math id="S4.p6.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma^{2}\subset M^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>⊂</mo><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma^{2}\subset M^{4}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The homology class of <math id="S4.p6.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math> in <math id="S4.p6.m29" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> is then Poincaré dual to <math id="S4.p6.m30" class="ltx_Math" alttext="mc_{1}(M,\omega)\in H^{2}(M,{\mathbb{Z}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ℤ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">mc_{1}(M,\omega)\in H^{2}(M,{\mathbb{Z}})</annotation></semantics></math>, while its
homology class in <math id="S4.p6.m31" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> is Poincaré dual to <math id="S4.p6.m32" class="ltx_Math" alttext="mc_{1}^{\rm orb}(X,J)\in H^{2}(X,{\mathbb{Q}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>orb</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ℚ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">mc_{1}^{\rm orb}(X,J)\in H^{2}(X,{\mathbb{Q}})</annotation></semantics></math>. The self-intersection
<math id="S4.p6.m33" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\Sigma]\cdot[\Sigma]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\Sigma]\cdot[\Sigma]</annotation></semantics></math> therefore computes both <math id="S4.p6.m34" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m^{2}c_{1}^{2}(M,\omega)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m^{2}c_{1}^{2}(M,\omega)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.p6.m35" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m^{2}c_{1}^{2}(X,J)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m^{2}c_{1}^{2}(X,J)</annotation></semantics></math>, and we must consequently have
<math id="S4.p6.m36" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{1}^{2}(X,J)=c_{1}^{2}(M,\omega)=\langle p_{1}(\Lambda^{+}),M\rangle=(2\chi+3\tau)(M)\in\{1,\ldots,9\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{1}^{2}(X,J)=c_{1}^{2}(M,\omega)=\langle p_{1}(\Lambda^{+}),M\rangle=(2\chi+3\tau)(M)\in\{1,\ldots,9\}</annotation></semantics></math>,
where the final list of possible values follows immediately from Theorem <a href="#S4.Thmthm1" title="Theorem 4.1. ‣ 4 Constraints on Diffeotype ‣ Desingularizations of ConformallyKähler, Einstein Orbifolds" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p7.1" class="ltx_p">As a consequence, we now immediately obtain the following variation on a result of Odaka-Spotti-Sun <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.Thmthm3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_prop">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S4.Thmthm3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 4.3</span></span><span id="S4.Thmthm3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S4.Thmthm3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Suppose that the <math id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> Kähler-Einstein orbifold <math id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X^{4},J,g_{\infty})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>J</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X^{4},J,g_{\infty})</annotation></semantics></math>
is the Gromov-Hausdorff limit of an admissible sequence <math id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,g_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,g_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>
of smooth Einstein <math id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>-manifolds <math id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,g_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,g_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>. If a singular point of <math id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,J)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X,J)</annotation></semantics></math>
has a neighborhood modeled on <math id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{C}^{2}/\Gamma_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>ℂ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>/</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{C}^{2}/\Gamma_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, where
<math id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Gamma_{k}\subset U(2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>⊂</mo><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Gamma_{k}\subset U(2)</annotation></semantics></math>, then</span></p>
<table id="S4.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\Gamma_{k}|&lt;\frac{12}{(2\chi+3\tau)(M)}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mfrac><mn>12</mn><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\Gamma_{k}|&lt;\frac{12}{(2\chi+3\tau)(M)}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">In particular,
every singular point has <math id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Gamma_{k}={\mathbb{Z}}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Gamma_{k}={\mathbb{Z}}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> if <math id="S4.Thmthm3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(2\chi+3\tau)(M)\geq 4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>χ</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(2\chi+3\tau)(M)\geq 4</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.3" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="S4.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text">If <math id="S4.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> is the metric induced on <math id="S4.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{4}/\Gamma_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>/</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{4}/\Gamma_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> by the usual round metric on <math id="S4.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{4}</annotation></semantics></math>, then
the Bishop-Gromov inequality and Gauss-Bonnet imply that</span></p>
<table id="S4.Ex9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="32\pi^{2}c_{1}^{2}(X)=\int_{X}s^{2}_{g_{\infty}}d\mu_{g_{\infty}}&lt;\int_{S^{4}/\Gamma_{k}}s^{2}_{g_{0}}d\mu_{g_{0}}=\frac{24\cdot 8\pi^{2}\chi(S^{4})}{|\Gamma_{k}|}=\frac{32\pi^{2}\cdot 12}{|\Gamma_{k}|}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mn>32</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∫</mo><mi>X</mi></msub><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub></msub></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">&lt;</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∫</mo><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>/</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mn>24</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo
